properties.description:
A gap acknowledgement records a human judgement about specific text. Today its expiry is keyed on the gap id, which hashes the affected node IDS — so a review expires when the affected SET changes membership, and NEVER when the affected nodes change CONTENT. Found live on 2026-07-30 while promoting the planning axis: acknowledgements written on 2026-07-28 reading roughly deferred, scheduled for a later increment went on suppressing gaps for requirements that had since been accepted and were being worked, so two things Anthony had just committed to were invisible as open work. Sharper still, req:graph-indexes-snapshots' acknowledgement was still justifying a framing that had been removed an hour earlier — an accepted review left defending a requirement that no longer said that. THE REASON IT MATTERS, and why this is not cosmetic: a review outliving the wording it reviewed is worse than no review, because it reads as a human having agreed to something they never saw. The nearest working sibling is defect-side expiry-by-shape, which already does content-sensitive invalidation. Approved for build by Anthony 2026-07-30.

REPRODUCED AGAIN 2026-07-31, AND THE SECOND OCCURRENCE IS THE STRONGER EVIDENCE BECAUSE OF HOW IT AROSE. Anthony accepted four `unverified_capability` gaps that morning. The recorded rationale for all four asserted — wrongly — that THIS capability would expire the review if the capability were reworded; it is `planned`, not built, so nothing of the kind happens. Within the hour he asked for the recommendation-with-options behaviour to be cemented, and cap:gap-carries-a-reading was substantially rewritten: RENAMED, given three new shape obligations and a language rule, and its check rewritten with two new negative assertions. The acknowledgement carried across untouched and went on suppressing the gap, and `reviewed_gaps` now renders the OLD judgement against the NEW title — the failure visible in a single tool result.

WHAT THE SECOND OCCURRENCE ADDS BEYOND THE FIRST: the 2026-07-30 case was drift over DAYS, which is easy to dismiss as staleness nobody could reasonably catch. This one took UNDER AN HOUR, inside one session, with the same agent doing both the acknowledging and the rewriting — and it still went unnoticed until `detect_gaps` was run and the expected gap did not reappear. An agent that had just written the sentence "rewording expires this review" then reworded the capability and did not notice. That is not a memory failure that better discipline fixes; it is the case for computing the expiry.

AND IT NAMES THE DIAGNOSTIC WORTH BUILDING ALONGSIDE: the failure was detected only because someone predicted the gap would return and checked. A silent non-return is indistinguishable from a correct suppression, which is why this cannot be left to review discipline.
properties.name: A sign-off expires when the thing it judged is reworded, not only when the affected set changes
